sections.b: Psalm 82 is the clearest picture of the divine council in the Psalms. God takes his stand "in the assembly of El" and judges the "gods" for failing the weak and the poor (Psalm 82:1–4). His verdict: "I said, 'You are gods, / and sons of the Most High, every one of you.' / Yet you will die as humans die" (Psalm 82:6–7). Most modern scholars read the gods as the heavenly rulers of the nations (compare Deuteronomy 32:8–9 in the Greek and the Dead Sea Scrolls). The Targum and Rashi read human judges; the Talmud, Israel at Sinai. Jesus cites Psalm 82:6 in John 10:34, and 11QMelchizedek applies Psalm 82:1 to Melchizedek as heavenly judge.

In Psalm 89 the same council, "the gathering of the holy ones" and "the inner council of the holy ones", praises God, and none of "the sons of the gods" is his equal (Psalm 89:5–7). Where Psalm 82 shows the council on trial, Psalm 89 shows it in awe.

sections.h: Psalm 89: the promise sung and questioned
sections.b: Psalm 89 retells Nathan's oracle (2 Samuel 7) as a sworn covenant (Psalm 89:3–4, 19–37). It adds what 2 Samuel lacks: the words covenant and oath, the king as "firstborn" and "most high over the kings of the earth", and the moon as a faithful witness. It keeps the father's rod but extends it to all David's sons and the whole law (Psalm 89:30–32). Then it accuses God of renouncing that covenant (Psalm 89:38–45) and asks, "Where, Lord, are your first acts of loyal love, / the ones you swore to David on your faithfulness?" (Psalm 89:49). Isaiah 55:3 seems to answer with the same words; the New Testament applies the oath to Jesus (Acts 2:30; Acts 13:34).
sections.refs: Psalm 89:3–4; Psalm 89:19–37; Psalm 89:38–51; 2 Samuel 7:8–17; Isaiah 55:3; Acts 13:34

sections.b: Psalm 88 gives the fullest picture of the world of the dead in the Old Testament: Sheol, the pit, the grave, Abaddon, the dark, the deeps, the land of forgetting, and the shades (refa'im) who live there (Psalm 88:3–12). The dead are "cut off from your hand" and cannot tell of God's loyal love (Psalm 88:5, 11). The psalm's questions expect the answer no; Isaiah 26:19 and Daniel 12:2 later answer them with resurrection. Psalm 86:13 thanks God for rescue from "the lowest Sheol", and Psalm 89:48 says no one escapes "the hand of Sheol".

sections.h: Psalm 88: a lament with no turn
sections.b: Psalm 88 is the only lament in the Psalter that never turns to trust or praise. It ends with "my companions are the dark" (Psalm 88:18). It still begins "LORD, God of my rescue" and keeps praying day and night (Psalm 88:1, 9, 13), and that persistence is its faith.

Psalm 89 is the boldest community protest in the Psalms: after praising God's faithfulness and quoting his oath to David, it accuses God of breaking it (Psalm 89:38–45) and asks, "How long, LORD?" (Psalm 89:46). Ibn Ezra reports that a Spanish sage refused to read it. Psalm 83 and Psalm 85 are community laments of a more usual kind.

Psalm 89 uses hesed, "loyal love", seven times and emunah, "faithfulness", seven times. It begins "The LORD's acts of loyal love I will sing forever" and turns the same words into a question at the end (Psalm 89:1, 49). Psalm 85:10 pictures loyal love and faithfulness meeting, and Psalm 86:15 quotes God's name from Exodus 34:6, "great in loyal love and faithfulness".

sections.h: The second group of Korah psalms (84–85, 87–88)
sections.b: Book III has a second group of psalms of "the sons of Korah": 84, 85, 87 and 88, a counterpart to 42–49 in Book II. They long for the Temple (Psalm 84), pray for renewal (Psalm 85), celebrate Zion as mother of nations (Psalm 87), and cry from the pit (Psalm 88). Numbers 26:11 notes that "the sons of Korah did not die" with their ancestor; Chronicles makes their descendants singers and gatekeepers.
sections.refs: Psalm 84:0; Psalm 85:0; Psalm 87:0; Psalm 88:0; Numbers 26:11; 1 Chronicles 9:19

sections.h: Asaph, Heman and Ethan in Book III
sections.b: Book III names all three of David's chief musicians in Chronicles. Psalms 73–83 are Asaph's; Psalm 88 is Heman's; Psalm 89 is Ethan's. 1 Kings 4:31 also names Heman and Ethan the Ezrahites as famous sages whom Solomon surpassed, and Chronicles counts them as Levite singers (1 Chronicles 15:17–19).

sections.h: Gittith, mahalath leannoth, and the end of Book III
sections.b: The titles of 81 and 84 mention the gittith, perhaps a lyre from Gath or a winepress song (the Greek has "for the winepresses"). Psalm 88 has the double title of the sons of Korah and Heman, with "mahalath leannoth". The blessing in Psalm 89:52 is not part of the psalm but the doxology that closes Book III, as Psalm 41:13 and Psalm 72:18–19 close Books I and II.
sections.refs: Psalm 81:0; Psalm 84:0; Psalm 88:0; Psalm 89:52; Psalm 41:13; Psalm 72:18–19

sections.h: Psalm 84 and Psalm 87: longing for Zion, mother of nations
sections.b: Psalm 84 is the pilgrim's longing for God's house in Zion, the road leading "from strength to strength" (Psalm 84:7). Psalm 87 pictures Zion as the city where God registers foreign peoples, Egypt and Babylon, Philistia, Tyre and Cush, as born there (Psalm 87:4–6). The Greek calls her "Mother Zion", an image Paul uses for the Jerusalem above (Galatians 4:26).

Psalm 81 calls for the ram's horn at the new moon and the full moon of "our feast day" (Psalm 81:3), most likely the autumn feast that began on the fifteenth of the seventh month. Its oracle repeats the first commandment, as the law was read at Booths every seventh year (Deuteronomy 31:10–13). Psalm 84, with its early rain (Psalm 84:6), may also be an autumn pilgrimage song.

sections.h: The shofar in Psalm 81 and Psalm 89
sections.b: "At the new moon blow the ram's horn" (Psalm 81:3) is the verse the Talmud uses for the shofar of Rosh Hashanah, which it calls the day of judgment (Bavli Rosh Hashanah 8a–b). Psalm 89:15, "Happy the people who know the shout of worship!", is recited after the shofar is blown.

Psalm 88:11 is the only use of Abaddon in the Psalms: "Will anyone tell of your loyal love in the grave, / or of your faithfulness in Abaddon?" There it is simply a name for the place of the dead, beside Sheol and the grave.

Psalm 83 asks God to treat a coalition of ten nations like Midian and Sisera, like tumbleweed and straw (Psalm 83:9–15). The Roman Liturgy of the Hours omits it. Yet it names a purpose beyond defeat: "so they will search for your name, LORD", and "let them learn that you... you alone are Most High above all the earth" (Psalm 83:16, 18).

Psalm 89 ends with enemies mocking the anointed king at every step (Psalm 89:51). The Targum renders it as mockery of "the delay of the footsteps of your Messiah", and the Mishnah's phrase "in the footsteps of the Messiah" names the troubled time before he comes (Mishnah Sotah 9:15). In the Greek the line reads "the reproach of your christ", which Hebrews 11:26 echoes.

God promises David, "I, for my part, will make him firstborn, / most high over the kings of the earth" (Psalm 89:27). Israel is God's firstborn in Exodus 4:22; here the king is. Revelation 1:5 calls Jesus "the faithful witness, the firstborn from the dead, and the ruler of the kings of the earth", echoing Psalm 89:27 and Psalm 89:37.

Psalm 89:9–10 praises God as master of the swelling sea, who "crushed Rahab like one cut down in battle". Rahab is the sea monster of old and a name for Egypt (Psalm 87:4), so creation and exodus are heard together. The Targum explains: "Rahab, that is wicked Pharaoh".

Nathan's promise, "I will be a father to him, and he will be a son to me" (2 Samuel 7:14), becomes the king's prayer in Psalm 89:26: "You are my Father, / my God, the rock of my rescue." Psalm 82:6 calls the members of God's council "sons of the Most High", a title that makes their failure worse.

The Dead Sea Scroll 11QMelchizedek quotes Psalm 82:1, "God takes his stand in the assembly of El", and applies it to Melchizedek, pictured as a heavenly judge who will condemn Belial and his spirits at the end of days.

Psalm 82:6, "I said, 'You are gods, / and sons of the Most High, every one of you'", which Jesus quotes in John 10:34, became a key text for theosis. Athanasius wrote that the Son became human so that we might become divine, and the Orthodox speak of being made partakers of the divine nature (2 Peter 1:4). The Catholic Catechism uses the same language (Catechism 460). Lutheran and Reformed readers took the psalm's "gods" as rulers and judges, and Latter-day Saints cite it for exaltation. The psalm itself speaks of a heavenly council judged for injustice (see divine-council).
